slides.title: Onsoo should enter the US in 2027 with an Amazon-led launch: it is the only route that fits the board's financial rules, but it needs gates because payback depends on ad cost

paragraphs.text: Onsoo should enter the US in 2027 with an Amazon-led launch: it is the only route that fits the board's financial rules, but it needs gates because payback depends on ad cost
Enter the US in 2027, rather than scale up Japan
US K-beauty skincare is $3.6B, growing 17% a year (category: 5%), and 41% of it sells on Amazon.
The pilot shows demand: 64,800 units in six months at 4.5 stars, a $4.0M annualised run-rate, and 29% repeat (benchmark 31%).
Amazon-led gives $26.4M of US revenue in 2030 vs $7.0M of extra revenue from the Japan scale-up, with peak cash of only $1.9–3.2M.
Lead with Amazon, not a 600-door specialty-retail launch
Amazon-led passes all three financial tests: peak cash –$1.9M (cap $18M), payback in 2030, group margin never below 9.5%.
Retail-led fails all three on its own numbers: peak cash –$20.8M, no payback by 2030, group margin 4.5% in 2027.
Its key inputs do not hold: at Onsoo's 4% awareness, newcomers sell a median 2.6 units/door/week (plan: 4.5; delisting below 4.0), and the 1.3× halo rests on a correlation.
Launch with conditions, because three parts of the CEO's plan need changing
Payback holds only if ACoS ≤ 28.6%. At the 32% benchmark for brands this size, cash is still –$2.3M at end-2030, so set a 28% ACoS ceiling and hold a gate in March 2028.
Retail from 2029 at the planned cost would break payback and the margin floor. Enter retail after payback and above 20% awareness (not 15%).
No modeled route reaches $40M by 2030 inside the cash cap and payback rule. Keep the rules and move the $40M date to about 2032.
Decision for March 2027: approve the Amazon-led launch with a $4M cash envelope, a 28% ACoS ceiling and a gate in March 2028; defer specialty retail; move the $40M ambition to about 2032.
Source: Onsoo briefing pack (Tables 1–9, survey Sept 2026); team analysis. Cash figures are pre-tax, cumulative US cash flow 2027–2030 incl. inventory.

paragraphs.text: Why the US wins the 2027 slot
Scale: the US adds about 4× the revenue Japan does by 2030, and is still growing 29% a year in 2030.
Bounded downside: even the worst US case tested (–$7.1M) uses under 40% of the $18M cap.
Timing: the pilot has momentum and 2,140 reviews. Waiting a year cedes a market growing 17% a year.
The trade-off
Japan is the safer bet for 2030 cash (+$1.8M vs –$2.3M at benchmark ACoS). We give that up for the only option that moves the US ambition forward.
The bandwidth limit covers 2027 only, so we recommend looking at the Japan scale-up again for 2028.
So what: use 2027 for the US. Japan's extra cash does not make up for losing a year in a market growing 17% a year, and the US downside is small.
Source: briefing pack Tables 5–7, group context; team model. Japan: incremental figures as given (no working-capital data provided). Stall case: Amazon flat at 200k units ($4.8M) a year at 32% ACoS.

data: Freight to US warehouse / retailer DC

paragraphs.text: Retail's own break-even, at the planned cost base
Retail-only fixed cost: $6.0M national marketing + $1.5M field team = $7.5M a year.
Units needed = $7.5M ÷ $7.545 = 994k a year. Across 600 doors that is ÷ (600 × 52) = 32 units/door/week.
The plan assumes 4.5; the evidence for Onsoo suggests 2.6. At 4.5, retail would need ≈4,248 doors to cover its costs.
At 4.5 units/door/week, 600 doors sell 140k units: $2.0M of wholesale revenue against $7.5M of fixed cost.
Amazon's sensitivity is advertising
Each ACoS point costs $0.24 a unit, or ≈ $0.67M over the 2.81M units planned for 2027–30.
Unit break-even ACoS is 44.7%, but covering fixed costs by 2030 needs ≤ 28.6% (see section 3).
So what: retail only makes sense if it lifts Amazon sales enough to pay for itself. That rests on the halo assumption tested on page 10.
Source: briefing pack Table 4 (Rice Ferment Barrier Cream, applied to all SKUs as the planning team does), Table 6. Contribution before fixed costs; duty at 15% of ex-factory cost.

slides.title: The 1.3× Amazon "halo" behind retail-led rests on a correlation; to pay for retail's costs the halo would need to be 2.1–3.4× from 2028

paragraphs.text: 1  Enter in 2027
2  Lead with Amazon
3  Launch with conditions
The 1.3× Amazon "halo" behind retail-led rests on a correlation; to pay for retail's costs the halo would need to be 2.1–3.4× from 2028
Why a 0.71 correlation does not show that retail drives Amazon
Reverse causation: retailers sign brands that already sell. Saebom reached ~$30M on Amazon first and then added 300 doors in 2025.
Common cause: older, bigger, better-funded brands have both more doors and more Amazon sales.
Survivorship: the sample is 30 brands sold in the US today. Failures such as Mooncrest are probably not in it.
Size of effect: r = 0.71 means r² ≈ 0.50 shared variance. It says nothing about direction or about how big a 1.3× uplift would be.
Customer evidence points the other way: only 17% of K-beauty buyers found their last new brand in a store (38% on TikTok), and 22% buy at specialty retail most often.
Amazon multiple needed for retail to cover its own costs

series.name: Amazon multiple needed to cover retail costs

paragraphs.text: Dashed orange line = the 1.3× halo assumed in Option B (a 30% uplift)
So what: the halo may exist, but it is unproven. To pay for retail it would have to lift Amazon sales by 110–240%, not 30%. Measure it before paying $7.5M a year for it.

Source: board member memo (r = 0.71 across 30 K-beauty brands), Table 9, survey Sept 2026. Halo needed = 1 + (retail fixed cost $7.5M – retail contribution) ÷ Option-A Amazon contribution at 25% ACoS; one-time costs excluded.

slides.title: Payback by 2030 is the binding constraint: Amazon-led pays back only if ACoS stays at or below 28.6%, while the benchmark for brands this size is 32%

paragraphs.text: 1  Enter in 2027
2  Lead with Amazon
3  Launch with conditions
Payback by 2030 is the binding constraint: Amazon-led pays back only if ACoS stays at or below 28.6%, while the benchmark for brands this size is 32%
Option A cumulative cash at end-2030 by ACoS (blue = pays back, red = does not)
Cumulative cash at end-2030, $M: ACoS × volume

The plan assumes ACoS falls to 25% as the brand matures. The agency data says it rises as brands bid on broader keywords, to a median of 32% between $5M and $20M a year, which is exactly A's path ($7.2M → $26.4M).
At the pilot's 28%, volume must reach ≥ 96% of plan to pay back. At 25%, ≥ 79%.
The cash cap is never the issue: peak cash stays between –$1.9M and –$6.4M across 25–38% ACoS.
So what: treat ACoS as the key operating metric. Cap blended ACoS at 28%, and give up growth rather than buy volume above the ceiling. Re-forecast at 32% before launch.
Source: team model; briefing pack §6 (pilot ACoS 28%), §11 (agency benchmark: median 32%, range 26–38% for brands scaling $5M→$20M on Amazon US). Volumes as planned unless stated.

The downside is bounded: even if sales stall or tariffs rise, Amazon-led needs at most $7.1M of peak cash, well under the $18M cap, and group margin stays above the 8% floor
Peak US cash need by scenario, $M (blue = Amazon-led; orange = retail-led for comparison)
$18M cap

If sales stall and we stop at the March 2028 gate, the loss is about $3M (2027: –$2.6M, plus one quarter of 2028). A 10% weaker won (≈ –$0.40 a unit) would roughly offset the tariff rise (+$0.35 a unit).
So what: the cash cap and margin floor are safe in every Amazon-led case. The real risk is payback. A gate can limit the cost of a stall to about $3M.

Source: team model. Tariff stress applies 25% duty to all years (decision expected mid-2027, so conservative). Stall = Gaon Lab/Yeoreum-type outcome (<$5M US revenue). FX: 10% weaker won cuts ex-factory + duty by ≈$0.40 a unit.

slides.title: Appendix: interpretation choices and key modeling assumptions

paragraphs.text: Appendix: interpretation choices and key modeling assumptions
Choices made where we would have asked
"$40M by 2030" is read as a 2030 revenue target and treated as an ambition. The cash cap, payback and margin floor are treated as hard constraints.
US revenue = what Onsoo receives: $24 on Amazon and $14 wholesale for retail, not shelf value.
Retail volumes run for the full year from 2027, as the planning team implies; no ramp-up.
Tariff stress applies 25% duty to all four years (conservative, since the decision is mid-2027).
Listings move from the cross-border seller to Onsoo's own operation inside the $0.8M setup cost.
Stall case = Amazon flat at 200k units ($4.8M) a year, consistent with peers below $5M.
Cash envelope $4M is our proposal, covering the worst non-stall stress case (–$3.9M).
Modeling conventions
Pre-tax US cash flow; constant FX (KRW 1,380/$); no terminal value.
Cash = units × unit contribution – fixed costs – one-time costs – change in inventory.
Inventory = 4 months of landed cost (ex-factory + freight + duty): $4.575 a unit on Amazon, $4.775 in retail.
Door fixtures ($1,100 per new door) expensed in the year the door opens.
Group margin = (ex-US plan revenue × 11% + US operating result) ÷ (ex-US revenue + US revenue). Inventory is excluded from the margin.
Hero-SKU unit economics applied to all SKUs, as the planning team does.
Japan (Option J): incremental revenue × 30% – $0.8M fixed – $1.0M one-time; no working-capital data provided.
Peak cash = the most negative cumulative cash position, 2027–30.
All inputs come from the briefing pack; no outside data used. Figures are synthetic benchmark data.

slides.title: Appendix: Option J (Japan scale-up) is low-risk and pays back in 2029, but adds only $7M of revenue by 2030

paragraphs.text: Appendix: Option J (Japan scale-up) is low-risk and pays back in 2029, but adds only $7M of revenue by 2030
Option J · incremental revenue × 30% contribution; $0.8M fixed a year; $1.0M one-time in 2027
Key calculations used in the deck
Amazon contribution = 24.00 – 3.60 referral – 5.10 FBA – 3.50 product – 0.55 freight – 0.525 duty = $10.725 before ads; – 25% × $24 = $4.725.
Retail contribution = 14.00 – 3.50 – 0.75 – 0.525 – 1.12 co-op – 0.56 returns = $7.545; break-even at 600 doors = 7.5M ÷ 7.545 ÷ 31,200 = 31.9 units/door/week.
Break-even ACoS for 2030 payback: cumulative contribution must cover $9.2M of fixed and setup costs plus $1.68M of end-2030 inventory over 2.81M units → $3.87 a unit → ACoS ≤ 28.6%.
